messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "The shared studio access list is maintained by the members of Alder Street Workshop, a fictional cooperative in a converted printing shop at 18 Alder Street. The list identifies who may enter the building, which rooms each person can use, and when an individual’s access expires. It is kept in a locked cabinet beside the reception desk, with a read-only copy on the studio’s internal network. The paper copy is the reference during an internet outage. Mara Venn, the studio coordinator, checks the two versions at the start of each month and records the date of the comparison on the cabinet log.

The building has a front entrance, a ceramics room, a woodshop, a photography room, and a small archive. Members receive a numbered badge for the front entrance and, where their work requires it, separate keys for restricted rooms. The access list records badge numbers rather than home addresses or personal phone numbers. It includes each member’s preferred name, the date access began, the approved areas, any scheduled access window, and the name of the person who authorized the entry. Emergency contacts are stored separately in a sealed envelope, so they are not visible to people reviewing routine access changes.

A new member does not receive a badge merely by appearing on the list. The member first completes an orientation with a trained host, signs the building-use agreement, and asks the relevant room steward to approve any restricted-room access. Once those steps are complete, Mara adds the member’s details and issues a badge. The record distinguishes the date the request was submitted from the date access actually begins. That distinction matters when someone joins during a busy week but cannot attend orientation until the following Monday.

The list is divided into three numbered sections:
1. Current members: names, badge numbers, approved rooms, and access dates.
2. Temporary access: visiting artists, repair workers, and collaborators, with a named host and a specific end date.
3. Returned or suspended credentials: badge numbers, the date they stopped working, and the reason for the change.

Each section has a separate update log. When a badge is lost, the member reports it to Mara or the building manager, who disables the badge before a replacement is issued. The log notes the report time and the time access was disabled. If the report comes after the building manager’s office has closed, the member must call the overnight security desk; the desk can disable the front-door credential but cannot authorize entry to a restricted room. That limitation is written beside the emergency number on the cabinet door.

Temporary access is limited to the dates and areas recorded for the visitor. For example, a repair technician may enter the woodshop on Thursday morning to inspect the dust collector, but that does not grant access to the ceramics room or permission to return on Friday. The host must remain in the building while the visitor is working. If a repair takes longer than expected, the host requests an extension from Mara before the listed end time; the visitor cannot extend the entry by writing a new date on a paper copy.

Some members use the photography room after the front desk closes. Their access is allowed only if the evening caretaker has confirmed that the alarm schedule will accommodate the session. This condition matters when Mara reviews a request for late access: a member’s current badge does not override the caretaker’s confirmation requirement. The caretaker’s name and the approved time window are recorded in the access log, while details of the member’s photographic project are not. If confirmation is unavailable, the session is moved to an open studio period rather than treated as approved.

Mara and the room stewards review restricted-room entries every quarter. During the review, they check whether a member still needs access, whether required safety training is current, and whether a key has been returned after a project ends. A person may remain a current studio member while losing permission to use one room; the list records that change without deleting the person’s other approved access. The steward adds a dated note describing the access decision, and Mara updates the active copy only after the steward has signed the review.

At the monthly member meeting, Mara gives a brief account of changes without reading out badge numbers or discussing private contact details. “The list should tell us who can enter and what they are authorized to use,” she said at the spring meeting. “It should not become a record of every conversation about someone’s work.” Members can report an error to Mara in person or through the locked suggestion box near reception. She checks the report against the update log and contacts the relevant steward when a correction concerns a restricted room.

The paper list is replaced when a page becomes difficult to read or when a scheduled review changes several entries. Old copies are marked with the date they were withdrawn and placed in a locked records drawer; they are not left beside the current list. At the end of each year, Mara and the cooperative’s elected secretary check that expired visitor entries have been removed from the active copy and that returned badges are accounted for. The secretary records any unresolved discrepancy for the next meeting, rather than assuming that a missing badge has been returned.

The access list supports daily operations, but it does not replace the building-use agreement, safety training records, or the incident log. If an alarm sounds, staff follow the posted emergency procedure and do not use the list to decide whether a person should be helped. If a member disputes an entry, Mara keeps the existing restriction in place until the responsible steward reviews the request; she does not change the record based only on a verbal disagreement.
